title: Pantone Color of the Year 2026: PANTONE 11-4201 Cloud Dancer
excerpt: Each year, the Pantone Color of the Year reflects broader cultural, social, and design shifts shaping how we live and interact with our environments. For 2026, PANTONE 11-4201 Cloud Dancer emerges as a subtle yet powerful…
body:
Each year, the Pantone Color of the Year reflects broader cultural, social, and design shifts shaping how we live and interact with our environments. For 2026, PANTONE 11-4201 Cloud Dancer emerges as a subtle yet powerful expression of calm, clarity, and balance.
Cloud Dancer is a refined off-white tone that responds to a growing desire for lightness and reassurance in interior spaces. Neither stark nor decorative, it offers a quiet neutrality that supports well-being while allowing form, texture, and materiality to take centre stage.
Why Cloud Dancer Matters for Property Presentation
In Home Staging, property development, and real estate marketing, colour plays a critical role in shaping first impressions and emotional responses. Cloud Dancer’s understated warmth makes it particularly effective as a foundational colour in residential interiors.
When applied thoughtfully, this tone enhances natural light, supports visual flow, and creates a sense of openness — all key factors in helping buyers feel comfortable and connected within a space. Its versatility allows architectural features, furnishings, and finishes to stand out without visual competition, reinforcing a cohesive and contemporary aesthetic.
A Strategic Neutral for Long-Term Appeal
Unlike trend-driven colours that can date quickly, Cloud Dancer offers longevity. Its adaptability makes it suitable across a wide range of property types, markets, and styles, supporting consistency and reducing the risk of trend fatigue. This makes it especially valuable for professionals seeking to balance current design relevance with broad buyer appeal.
Translating Colour Trends into Professional Practice
The Pantone Color of the Year should be viewed not as a directive, but as insight. For industry professionals, Cloud Dancer provides guidance on evolving buyer preferences — favouring calm, clarity, and thoughtful simplicity over visual noise.
Used with intention, it can support stronger property narratives, enhance emotional connection, and contribute to spaces that feel both welcoming and aspirational.

title: GAPHS Appoints Rita de Miranda as Regional Director for Portugal
excerpt: We are proud to announce the appointment of Rita de Miranda as Regional Director for Portugal, recognizing her outstanding contribution to the professionalization of Home Staging and real estate presentation in the Portuguese…
body:
We are proud to announce the appointment of Rita de Miranda as Regional Director for Portugal, recognizing her outstanding contribution to the professionalization of Home Staging and real estate presentation in the Portuguese market.

A pioneer of Home Staging in Portugal, Rita de Miranda introduced the discipline to the national real estate industry at a time when it was virtually unknown. In 2011, she became the first Portuguese professional certified by Home Staging Resource (USA) and a member of the American Society of Home Stagers and Redesigners, marking the beginning of a transformative journey for the sector.

Driven by a strong commitment to education and professional standards, Rita developed the first Home Staging training programs for real estate professionals in Portugal, collaborating with leading national and international real estate brands. Today, she is the most experienced Home Staging trainer in the country, having trained more than 10,000 students and completed over 350 Home Staging projects.

Rita is the Founder and President of APHS, Associação Portuguesa de Home Stagers, established in 2021, through which she became the only trainer worldwide certifying Home Staging professionals in Portuguese across three levels: National, European, and International. In 2024, she further expanded access to education by founding the Home Staging Academy, offering specialized programs for different stages of professional development across the Portuguese-speaking community.

Her work and leadership have earned international recognition. In 2022, Rita was personally invited by Barb Schwarz, creator of Home Staging, to join her list of recommended Home Stagers, becoming the first Portuguese professional to receive this distinction. She is also a published author, contributor to reference publications in the real estate sector, and a frequent speaker at national and international conferences.

With her appointment as GAPHS Regional Director for Portugal, Rita de Miranda will play a key role in strengthening professional standards, fostering education, and supporting the growth of the Home Staging industry within the global GAPHS network.

This appointment not only acknowledges Rita’s exceptional career, but also represents an important step forward for the continued development and international recognition of Home Staging in Portugal.

title: Home Staging: The Real Definition Beyond Aesthetics
excerpt: Despite its growing visibility, Home Staging is still widely misunderstood. Too often, it is reduced to decoration or superficial styling, when in reality it is a strategic, performance-driven discipline positioned at the…
body:
Despite its growing visibility, Home Staging is still widely misunderstood. Too often, it is reduced to decoration or superficial styling, when in reality it is a strategic, performance-driven discipline positioned at the intersection of real estate marketing, communication, and buyer psychology.

At its core, Home Staging is a professional methodology designed to enhance a property’s market performance by improving how it is perceived, understood, and emotionally experienced by potential buyers.

Home Staging as a Real Estate Marketing Tool

Home Staging functions as a results-oriented real estate marketing tool because it directly influences key performance indicators within the sales process.

Professionally staged properties:
        •        Attract higher online and in-person engagement
        •        Generate more qualified buyer interest
        •        Spend less time on the market compared to unstaged properties

By reducing visual and functional uncertainty, Home Staging accelerates buyer decision-making and strengthens the perceived value of the property. Buyers are able to immediately understand the space, its potential, and its positioning within the market.

This clarity leads to:
        •        Fewer price reductions
        •        Stronger negotiation positions
        •        In many cases, higher final sale prices compared to similar, non-staged properties

Home Staging does not inflate value artificially; rather, it reveals value clearly and coherently, allowing the property to compete effectively and fairly within its market segment.

Home Staging as a Communication Tool

Beyond marketing metrics, Home Staging is fundamentally a powerful communication tool.

It translates the property’s potential into a visual language that buyers instantly understand, without the need for explanation. Layouts become legible, proportions clear, and functions intuitive. By eliminating ambiguity and cognitive effort, Home Staging removes visual confusion and helps buyers grasp how the space works the moment they enter.

At the same time, Home Staging creates an emotional connection. Through carefully guided light, flow, balance, and atmosphere, it allows buyers to move beyond observing square meters and begin imagining a lifestyle.

Instead of seeing a house, buyers start to envision themselves living there — and this emotional engagement is one of the strongest drivers of purchasing decisions.

Framing Value and Reducing Perceived Risk

Home Staging also plays a crucial role in framing the property correctly within its market context.

By reinforcing coherence, quality, and care, it communicates that the property has been professionally prepared, positioned, and valued. This visual narrative:
        •        Supports pricing strategies
        •        Reduces buyer resistance
        •        Lowers perceived risk
        •        Strengthens confidence in the value being offered

When buyers feel secure in their understanding of a property, they are more likely to make confident, timely decisions.

More Than Design: A Strategic Discipline

Home Staging is not decoration, nor is it interior design for personal taste. It is a strategic discipline that combines market analysis, spatial communication, and emotional intelligence to serve a clear objective: helping properties sell faster, more efficiently, and at their true market value.

Understanding this distinction is essential for real estate professionals, sellers, and investors who wish to operate at a higher professional standard in today’s competitive market.

At GAPHS, we continue to promote clarity, education, and excellence in Home Staging worldwide—ensuring that the discipline is recognized for what it truly is: a strategic asset in modern real estate.

Article by Sanja Radovanovic
President GAPHS

title: The Measurable Impact of Home Staging on the Italian Real Estate Market
excerpt: In January 2025, a national survey conducted in Italy engaged a wide spectrum of real estate professionals, home stagers, and industry operators. The significant level of participation ensured the collection of reliable and…
body:
In January 2025, a national survey conducted in Italy engaged a wide spectrum of real estate professionals, home stagers, and industry operators. The significant level of participation ensured the collection of reliable and representative data, offering a clear and updated overview of the role of Home Staging within the Italian property market.

Data That Speaks Clearly

The survey results provide concrete evidence not only in terms of reduced time on market but also in improved financial performance. When compared with official figures published by the Italian Ministry of Economy and Finance – OMI (Real Estate Market Observatory), the difference is substantial.

According to OMI data:
        •        Average selling time: 175 days
        •        Average discount on asking price: 7.5%

According to the survey findings for properties enhanced through targeted Home Staging interventions:
        •        Average selling time: 30 days
        •        Average discount on asking price: 3%

Strategic Value and Profitability

These results demonstrate a dramatic reduction in marketing time alongside stronger price retention. The financial implications are clear: faster sales cycles and minimized negotiations directly enhance transaction profitability.

In a market where competition is increasing and first impressions decisively influence purchasing decisions, strategic property presentation confirms itself as a fundamental success factor.

Property enhancement consolidates its position as one of the highest-return investments applicable to a property for sale. For owners, investors, and real estate professionals, Home Staging represents a measurable, data-driven lever capable of maximizing both performance and return on investment.

title: How to successfully enter the luxury home staging segment?
excerpt: For many home stagers, the luxury market is the ultimate ambition. We dream of staging penthouses with breathtaking city views, majestic canal houses, or expansive villas. But while these high-end projects are the pinnacle of…
body:
For many home stagers, the luxury market is the ultimate ambition. We dream of staging penthouses with breathtaking city views, majestic canal houses, or expansive villas. But while these high-end projects are the pinnacle of our profession, securing and successfully executing them requires a specific approach. It takes more than just a beautiful eye; it requires a deep understanding of the nuances that define the premium segment.

At first glance, it might seem that luxury staging requires a more expensive inventory. In reality, the difference between a standard project and a high-end presentation is far more deliberate. Luxury is not about quantity; it is a study in precision, restraint, and intention.

Luxury is about restraint, not abundance

A common misconception in the industry is that luxury requires "more", more accessories, more layers, more visible opulence. In the high-end segment, the opposite is often true.

Premium properties demand space. Architectural lines and high-quality materials need room to breathe. Overstyling can unintentionally diminish a home's perceived value. In this segment, restraint signals confidence. Every piece must justify its presence; if it doesn't serve the narrative, it doesn't belong in the room. This requires the discipline to choose pieces that can stand alone without visual noise.

The language of texture and materiality

Luxury staging is less about bold color statements and more about depth and tactile richness. Natural materials, honed stone, heavy linen, raw wood, and brushed metals, create a sense of quality that buyers feel before they even consciously analyze it. The difference often lies in the "finish": the weight of a drape, the grain of a side table, or the pile of a silk-blend rug. In premium real estate, you aren't just staging a house; you are curating a Lifestyle. Your staging must meet the high expectations of a buyer used to the best.

Anchoring the space with statement pieces

In the higher segment, a single, well-chosen statement piece can anchor an entire room. This might be a sculptural armchair, a bespoke lighting fixture, or a large-scale artwork that elevates the space beyond the predictable.

These pieces don't need to be loud, but they must be intentional. Having access to unique, high-quality furniture allows a stager to create memorability. When a potential buyer views five properties in one afternoon, they won't remember the filler, they will remember the atmosphere you created.

Precision in execution is non-negotiable

In luxury, the "how" is just as important as the "what." Furniture placement must feel effortless, proportions must be mathematically sound, and lines must be impeccably clean. There is zero margin for error, rushed setups, or logistical compromises.

Furthermore, high-end listings often follow strict marketing timelines. A seamless, professional installation process reflects directly on your brand. When the logistics are handled with military precision, you, as the stager, can remain focused on the creative and strategic heart of the project.

Scaling into luxury without the overhead

The ambition to move into the luxury segment often brings up practical hurdles:

“Do I need to invest heavily in a new, expensive inventory?”

“How do I maintain flexibility while elevating my quality?”

The answer isn't necessarily owning more; it’s about organizing your resources differently. Strategic collaboration is the key to scaling. By partnering with a specialist who offers an up-to-date, premium collection and full logistical support, from white-glove transport to installation, you can deliver luxury-level results without the burden of fixed costs.

The Staging Company empowers home stagers to operate confidently in the high-end market. We provide access to distinctive interior pieces and professional logistical execution, acting as an extension of your team. This doesn’t replace your creative identity; it provides the foundation for it to flourish.

Luxury is clarity

Ultimately, luxury staging isn’t defined by a price tag or square footage. It is defined by a clarity of concept and a relentless focus on detail.

For stagers looking to grow, the question isn’t how much you own, but how you leverage the right partnerships to deliver at a higher level consistently. Luxury isn’t louder, it is more deliberate. And that deliberate approach is exactly what makes the difference.

Design without limits

Are you ready to elevate your portfolio and confidently step into the high-end market? Moving into luxury doesn't mean you have to go it alone. The Staging Company is more than an inventory provider; we are your strategic partner in excellence. From active collaboration on layout and material selection to flawless, professional execution, we provide the foundation your creative vision deserves.

title: Advancing professional standards in Georgia: REAL ESTATE PRO DAY in Tbilisi
excerpt: On 12 March 2026, a significant educational initiative for the real estate sector took place in Tbilisi with the organisation of REAL ESTATE PRO DAY - Modern Methods of Preparing Property for Sale.
body:
On 12 March 2026, a significant educational initiative for the real estate sector took place in Tbilisi with the organisation of REAL ESTATE PRO DAY - Modern Methods of Preparing Property for Sale.

The event was presented by the International Chamber of Commerce Georgia in partnership with the GNARE – Georgian National Association of Real Estate and supported by the GAPHS – Global Association of Property & Home Staging Professionals. The initiative was curated and led by Marika Abuashvili, whose work focuses on aligning international best practices with the evolving Georgian market.

A structured approach to modern real estate marketing

The intensive programme was designed to provide real estate professionals with practical tools and a structured understanding of contemporary property marketing. The training focused on three core areas: building client trust and securing exclusive listings, presenting properties effectively through Home Staging, and understanding the strategic role of the Open House within the sales process.
Particular attention was given to visual marketing and professional Home Staging as key elements in increasing perceived property value and improving sales performance without relying on price reductions. This reflects a broader international trend in which presentation, positioning, and visual communication play an increasingly strategic role in real estate.

Recognising the pioneers of professional Home Staging in Georgia

The programme also highlighted the contribution of professionals who are actively introducing Home Staging to the Georgian market. Among the speakers were Dina Semenenko, founder of Georgia’s first professional home staging business and a GAPHS member, and Olga Suslova, founder of the proptech platform Inframe.ge and a specialist in high-end property visualisation.

Their participation contributed to strengthening awareness of how professional staging and visual communication can support agents, developers, and investors in positioning properties more effectively and building stronger relationships with clients.

A step forward for the professional development of the market

Initiatives such as REAL ESTATE PRO DAY represent an important step in the ongoing development of the real estate sector in Georgia. By encouraging the adoption of international standards and promoting collaboration between real estate professionals, visual marketing experts, and home stagers, the event contributed to a more structured and forward-looking market environment.

title: From inventory-driven to project-driven: a smarter business model for home staging businesses
excerpt: Most home stagers believe success begins with building inventory. But this belief is rarely questioned.
body:
Most home stagers believe success begins with building inventory. But this belief is rarely questioned.

Furniture.
Accessories.
Storage space.

A collection that reflects your style and allows you to take on projects independently.
This inventory-driven approach feels safe. Yet, relying on familiarity and control can blind you to opportunity.

Is your growth truly as logical as it seems?
Or is it based on assumptions holding you back?
Does sticking to inventory keep you from landing high-end projects and bigger opportunities?
Is accumulating assets really the lowest-risk, most adaptive route to business growth?
Does it propel you forward, or keep you stagnant?

The inventory-driven model
An inventory-driven business model is built around ownership.
You invest in furniture and accessories, build your own collection, and create a storage structure around it. Projects are planned based on what is available in your inventory.

On the surface, this is a logical and practical way to build a home staging business. Especially in the early stages, or when working on smaller, lower-segment properties, it allows you to move quickly and operate independently. A well-curated base collection can take you a long way in this segment.

However, as soon as you start aiming for larger or more exclusive projects, the model becomes significantly more complex.

Higher-end staging requires a different level of quality, variation, and uniqueness. And this is where ownership starts to create limitations. Many luxury brands do not work with small, project-based buyers or require minimum purchase volumes. At the same time, the types of pieces needed for high-end staging often come with a substantial price tag.

Building an inventory that can consistently support luxury-level projects requires a major upfront investment, often far beyond what is realistic or efficient for a single home-staging business.

As a result, the inventory-driven model tends to work best within a certain range of projects. It is effective for smaller, more standardized assignments where a fixed collection can be used repeatedly, but it becomes increasingly difficult to scale into higher segments without significantly increasing risk and capital investment.

On top of that, inventory brings structural considerations. Storage becomes a fixed cost. Availability becomes a planning constraint. And occupancy starts to play a role. When projects are running, your inventory is in use. When they are not, it remains idle.
Seasonality can amplify this effect. Busy periods may require additional investment, while quieter periods can leave valuable assets unused.

This model isn’t wrong. But it locks you into rigidity, limiting your ability to pursue bigger ambitions.

The project-driven alternative
A project-driven model approaches the business from a different angle.
Instead of building the business around what you own, build it around what each project requires.

Costs move with each project, freeing you from static expenses. Adapt to shifting demand and seize new opportunities.

This method unlocks projects that others only dream of. Flexibility in size, style, and segment becomes your advantage.

Rather than expanding inventory as the business grows, you expand your ability to deliver projects.

Risk distribution and financial flexibility
One of the key differences between the two models lies in how risk is managed.
In an inventory-driven model, a significant portion of capital is tied up in physical assets. These assets need to be stored, maintained, and utilized to justify the investment.
With project-driven costs aligning with revenue, you are free to grow without pressure. Quiet periods no longer threaten your business.

It also allows for different types of investment. Instead of allocating capital to additional inventory, resources can be directed towards marketing, branding, or business development.
This perspective is relevant for both new and established home stagers. For those starting out, it lowers the barrier to entry. For those already operating, it provides an alternative way to scale without increasing fixed costs.

Building a scalable ecosystem
A project-driven approach is rarely built in isolation. It often relies on collaboration and a broader home staging ecosystem.

Instead of owning every component of the process, home staging professionals work with partners who provide specific expertise and infrastructure. This can include access to furniture collections, logistics, transport, installation, and dismantling.
This type of collaboration shifts the focus from ownership to access.
Gain access to diverse, current collections, styles, and logistics.
Access to different styles and segments.
Access to a logistics system that is already in place.
It allows home staging professionals to remain flexible while still delivering at a high professional level.

The Staging Company supports home staging professionals in this ecosystem. By offering flexible rental per individual item, access to a broad and current collection, and a structured logistics system including transport, installation, and dismantling, it enables home staging professionals to operate in a project-driven way without carrying the full operational load themselves.

A shift in how growth is defined
Ultimately, the difference between an inventory-driven and a project-driven model is not just operational. It is strategic.

It changes how growth is defined.

Growth now means surpassing limits, delivering excellence, and responding fiercely to demand. Inventory size loses meaning.

The future of home staging is not necessarily about owning more.
It is about organizing smarter.

And for many home stagers, that shift can make the difference between a business that grows in complexity and one that grows in flexibility and opportunity

title: The Institutional Evolution of Home Staging in Greece: Professional Standards, International Cooperation, and Industry Integration
excerpt: The professional home staging industry continues to evolve globally through the development of structured standards, international collaboration, and increasing institutional recognition within the broader real estate sector.
body:
The professional home staging industry continues to evolve globally through the development of structured standards, international collaboration, and increasing institutional recognition within the broader real estate sector.

In Greece, these developments are being actively observed and supported through the work of professionals engaged in both international and regional industry organizations. Among them is Yuliia Fareniuk, GAPHS Member and Representative in Greece, who has been contributing to the development and visibility of the home staging profession within the Greek market since January 2024. Since March 2025, she has also been a member of the FIABCI Greece Chapter, further strengthening the connection between home staging and the wider international real estate community.

Participation in professional associations and international assemblies provides valuable insight into the ongoing institutionalization of the profession, including the establishment of membership criteria, professional standards, qualification systems, and mechanisms of professional verification.

Institutionalization of Professional Standards

On 27 February 2026, the General Assembly of the Global Association of Professional Home Stagers (GAPHS) adopted Amendment 4.1, introducing further clarification regarding professional membership criteria within the association.

Under the updated provisions, professional membership is available to individuals who have successfully completed recognized professional education programs. This development reflects the industry’s broader movement toward structured qualification frameworks and clearly defined professional standards.

The implementation of formalized admission criteria contributes to greater transparency within the profession while supporting the establishment of consistent educational and competency benchmarks for home staging professionals internationally.

As the industry continues to mature, professional associations increasingly play a central role in defining quality standards, promoting ethical practices, and reinforcing professional accountability.

Professional Participation and Industry Development

Active participation in professional organizations remains an essential component in the advancement of the home staging sector.

Engagement in assemblies, committees, working groups, and industry initiatives enables professionals to remain informed about regulatory developments, contribute to the evolution of professional standards, and align their practices with international expectations and market demands.

This level of professional integration supports the sustainable growth of the industry while reinforcing the credibility and long-term positioning of home staging within the real estate and property preparation sectors.

International Context: FIABCI and Cross-Industry Integration

On 21 March 2026, the General Assembly of the FIABCI Greece Chapter took place, bringing together professionals from multiple sectors of the international real estate industry.

As part of her participation within FIABCI Greece and representation of GAPHS, Yuliia Fareniuk contributed to discussions focused on professional structure, membership criteria, and standards of professional representation.

FIABCI, recognized globally as one of the leading international federations within the real estate sector, serves as a platform for interdisciplinary collaboration, knowledge exchange, and international professional networking.

Among the topics addressed during the assembly were:

•⁠  ⁠clarification of active membership and voting participation criteria

•⁠  ⁠reinforcement of the connection between professional activity and verified membership status

•⁠  ⁠discussion surrounding structured professional infrastructure as an indicator of organized professional practice

•⁠  ⁠development of internal verification mechanisms designed to maintain member quality, credibility, and professional reputation

These discussions reflect broader international trends toward increased transparency, professional accountability, and institutional strengthening across the real estate sector.

The Emergence of a Multi-Level Professional Structure

The ongoing evolution of home staging demonstrates the emergence of a multi-level professional ecosystem composed of both international and local institutional frameworks.

International associations provide professionals with access to unified standards, global best practices, educational resources, and coordinated approaches to professional qualification.

At the same time, regional and national organizations remain essential in addressing local market dynamics, regulatory environments, and culturally specific business practices.

The interaction between global standards and local implementation creates a balanced and sustainable model for professional development, supporting both industry consistency and regional adaptability.

Cooperation Between Professional Associations

Within the framework of the existing memorandum of cooperation between GAPHS and FIABCI, opportunities for professional collaboration and interdisciplinary engagement continue to expand.

This cooperation model allows eligible GAPHS members to access FIABCI membership pathways in accordance with established registration procedures and professional compliance requirements.

Such initiatives contribute to the creation of a more integrated professional environment while strengthening collaboration between the home staging industry and the broader international real estate sector.

The Ongoing Transformation of the Profession

Current industry developments indicate a clear transition of home staging from a predominantly individual entrepreneurial activity toward a more structured and institutionally recognized profession.

Key elements driving this transformation include:

•⁠  ⁠formalization of educational and qualification standards

•⁠  ⁠increasing influence of professional associations as standard-setting institutions

•⁠  ⁠expansion of international professional cooperation

•⁠  ⁠growing importance of verified professional status and accountability

Together, these developments are shaping a new professional architecture in which transparency, structured standards, and institutional credibility represent fundamental pillars of industry growth.

Conclusion

The global home staging industry is entering a new phase of professional evolution characterized by increased structure, stronger institutional frameworks, and growing international collaboration.

The expanding role of professional associations, alongside the development of unified membership standards and interdisciplinary cooperation, continues to strengthen the profession’s credibility and long-term sustainability within the international real estate market.

As these processes continue to evolve, they contribute not only to the professionalization of home staging, but also to greater recognition of its strategic value within modern real estate practice.

Yuliia Fareniuk
GAPHS Member and Representative in Greece
FIABCI Greece Chapter Member
Founder, Home Staging Services Greece E.E.

title: The hidden cost of doing everything yourself as a home stager - By The Home Staging Company
excerpt: Many home stagers start their businesses as solopreneurs. In the early stages, this approach feels natural and often necessary. You build your own collection, manage your own projects, and maintain full control over every…
body:
Many home stagers start their businesses as solopreneurs. In the early stages, this approach feels natural and often necessary. You build your own collection, manage your own projects, and maintain full control over every decision. Every piece of furniture, every accessory, and every detail of the staging reflects your personal vision.
For many professionals, this independence is part of the profession's appeal.
However, as the number of projects grows and the business becomes more established, a different question arises: What is the real cost of doing everything yourself?
At first, the cost seems merely financial. In truth, it also drains time, mental energy, and long-term capacity.
Time is your most limited asset.
Running a home staging business involves far more than the creative work itself. Styling a property may be the most visible part of the profession, but behind every finished project lies significant operational work.
Projects require careful planning. Furniture and accessories must be transported, installed, and then removed. Inventory must be tracked and maintained. Communication with clients, agents, and contractors must be managed. Unexpected scheduling or access changes often require quick adjustments.
Individually, each of these tasks may seem manageable. But together they create a complex operational layer beneath the creative side of the business.
As a home stager takes on more projects, operational work multiplies. Unlike inventory or storage, time can't be increased; there are only so many hours in a day.
Many times, time becomes the most valuable and limited business resource.
Creative energy versus operational energy
Home staging is ultimately a creative profession. The role of the home stager is to transform a property into a compelling visual narrative that helps potential buyers imagine a future in the space. Achieving this requires creativity, intuition, and a strong sense of spatial balance.
Creativity needs mental space.
Operational work demands something else entirely. Logistics, transport coordination, installation planning, and problem-solving require structure, precision, and close attention to detail.
When both types of work compete for mental energy, maintaining balance becomes difficult. A day beginning with creative planning can quickly shift to logistical problem-solving if a delivery is delayed or a schedule changes.
Constantly switching between creative and operational tasks can gradually reduce mental space for quality creative work.
Many home stagers recognise this tension but accept it as an unavoidable part of the profession.
Capacity ceilings: the invisible growth barrier
A major hidden cost of solo entrepreneurship is the hard cap it places on how much your business can grow, no matter your effort or dedication.
A single person can coordinate only a limited number of projects at once. As the number of assignments increases, the complexity of planning and logistics grows as well. Projects begin to overlap, schedules become tighter, and the margin for error becomes smaller.
At a certain point, the workload reaches a natural ceiling.
This is not always obvious. From the outside, the business may seem busy and successful. Internally, operational pressure rises, and the capacity to accept new opportunities shrinks.
More projects can boost revenue, but without structural support, they also increase stress, lengthen workdays, and reduce flexibility, making it harder to scale the business.
Professional support as a growth accelerator
For some home stagers, bringing in outside support can feel uncomfortable. Independence and control often define a creative entrepreneur's identity.
However, professional support does not necessarily mean losing control. In many cases, it simply means organising the business more strategically.
When operational elements are supported by professional infrastructure, workflows become more manageable. Logistics, transport, installation, and dismantling are handled in a structured, reliable manner, enabling smoother project execution.
This creates something that is often overlooked in a busy staging business: clarity.
With a reliable operational foundation, home stagers can more easily adapt to scheduling changes, manage multiple projects, and focus their energy where it matters most.
Instead of spending time on logistics, focus returns to styling, concept development, and compelling property presentations.
A professional partner can also shift your mindset. Even as an independent entrepreneur, you no longer face all operational challenges alone. You become part of a supportive ecosystem.
Making strategic choices as an entrepreneur
Every business reaches a point where strategic choices are required, especially regarding how much operational work to manage yourself.
Some home stagers prefer managing everything themselves. Others reorganise workflows to create space for growth, balance, and opportunities.
The Staging Company supports home stagers by providing access to an extensive, up-to-date furniture collection, along with a structured logistics system that includes transport, installation, and dismantling. By working alongside home stagers as a professional partner, it becomes easier to scale projects while maintaining focus on the creative and strategic aspects of the profession.
Doing everything yourself is often how the journey begins.
Building a scalable, sustainable business often starts with choosing which responsibilities to delegate, enabling you to overcome hidden growth barriers.

title: Insights from the First Global Home Staging Statistics Survey
excerpt: For decades, Home Staging professionals have shared success stories, case studies, and client testimonials demonstrating the value of property presentation. Yet until now, our industry lacked something fundamental: global data.
body:
For decades, Home Staging professionals have shared success stories, case studies, and client testimonials demonstrating the value of property presentation. Yet until now, our industry lacked something fundamental: global data.

In 2026, GAPHS (Global Association of Professional Home Stagers) launched the first Global Home Staging Statistics Survey, bringing together professionals from Europe and beyond to provide a snapshot of the industry’s current landscape.

While this inaugural survey represents the beginning of a larger benchmarking initiative, the results already reveal a profession that is maturing rapidly, diversifying its services, and delivering measurable impact on real estate performance.

A Truly International Profession

The survey gathered responses from Home Staging professionals operating across multiple countries, including Switzerland, Italy, Greece, Portugal, Spain, Poland, Ireland, Hungary, The Netherlands, Thailand, and Russia.

The geographical diversity of respondents demonstrates that Home Staging is no longer concentrated in a handful of mature markets. It is becoming a global profession with local adaptations, market-specific strategies, and growing recognition among real estate stakeholders.

Real Estate Professionals Remain the Primary Client

One of the strongest findings from the survey is the continued importance of the real estate industry as a source of business.

Most respondents identified real estate agents and agencies as their primary client segment, confirming that Home Staging is increasingly integrated into professional property marketing strategies.

At the same time, private investors, homeowners, and investment companies represent significant and growing client categories, suggesting that awareness of Home Staging’s value extends beyond traditional brokerage channels.

Home Staging Is Expanding Beyond Staging

The modern Home Stager is becoming a property presentation specialist.

Survey participants reported offering a wide range of complementary services, including:

•⁠  ⁠Interior Decorating
•⁠  ⁠Interior Design
•⁠  ⁠Short-Term Rental Design
•⁠  ⁠Color Consulting
•⁠  ⁠Professional Photography
•⁠  ⁠Furniture Rental
•⁠  ⁠Re-Design Services
•⁠  ⁠3D Rendering and Virtual Tours
•⁠  ⁠Open House Preparation
•⁠  ⁠Property Marketing Support

This diversification reflects a broader industry evolution where professionals are creating comprehensive solutions designed to maximize property appeal and market performance.

Vacant Staging Dominates Global Activity

Across most markets, vacant staging represents the majority of business activity.

Many respondents indicated that vacant staging accounts for between 60% and 100% of their projects.

This trend highlights the growing recognition that empty properties often struggle to communicate scale, functionality, and emotional appeal to potential buyers.

By transforming vacant spaces into aspirational environments, Home Stagers help buyers visualize lifestyle opportunities and make faster purchasing decisions.

Luxury Home Staging Is Growing

A significant percentage of respondents reported actively working within the luxury market.

Interestingly, the definition of “luxury” varies substantially across regions, with entry thresholds ranging from approximately €500,000 in some markets to more than €2 million in others.

Despite these differences, one common theme emerged: presentation becomes increasingly important as property value increases.

Luxury sellers, developers, and investors are increasingly using Home Staging as a strategic tool to support premium positioning and maximize market perception.

The Data Behind the Success Stories

Perhaps the most compelling findings come from the professional success stories shared by participants.

Across multiple countries and market segments, respondents consistently reported:

•⁠  ⁠Properties selling in days instead of months
•⁠  ⁠Significant reductions in Days on Market
•⁠  ⁠Multiple-offer situations
•⁠  ⁠Sales above asking price
•⁠  ⁠Rental income increases
•⁠  ⁠Strong returns on staging investment

Examples included:

•⁠  ⁠A property in Milan selling in 10 days after remaining on the market for 16 months.
•⁠  ⁠An Irish property achieving €205,000 above asking price after professional preparation.
•⁠  ⁠A Greek apartment generating a 1,500% return on staging investment.
•⁠  ⁠Multiple projects across Hungary reporting price increases between 15% and 30%.
•⁠  ⁠Properties in Spain, Portugal, Switzerland, and Italy selling within days of being staged after extended periods on the market.

While individual results vary by market, the consistency of outcomes across countries suggests that Home Staging contributes directly to stronger market performance when implemented strategically.

A Profession at Different Stages of Maturity

The survey also reveals an industry characterized by both experienced veterans and emerging entrepreneurs.

Respondents ranged from professionals with more than ten years of experience to newer businesses established within the last three years.

This balance is encouraging. It demonstrates that Home Staging continues to attract new professionals while retaining experienced practitioners who are helping shape industry standards and best practices.

Looking Ahead

The first GAPHS Global Home Staging Statistics Survey represents more than a collection of numbers.

It marks an important milestone in the professionalization of our industry.

For years, Home Stagers have known the value of what they do. Now we are beginning to quantify that value on a global scale.

As participation grows in future editions of the survey, GAPHS aims to create the world’s most comprehensive source of Home Staging industry data, helping professionals, real estate stakeholders, investors, and policymakers better understand the measurable impact of property presentation.

The message emerging from this first global benchmark is clear:

Home Staging is no longer simply about making properties look better.

It is about helping properties perform better.

And the data is beginning to prove it.

For the final publication, I would add a short presidential quote from you, something like:

“For many years, our industry has relied on anecdotes and individual case studies. This survey marks the beginning of something much larger: the creation of a global body of evidence that demonstrates the measurable impact of Home Staging on real estate performance worldwide.”

Sanja Radovanovic
President, GAPHS

title: What Makes a Professional Home Stager?
excerpt: What Makes a Professional Home Stager?
body:
What Makes a Professional Home Stager?

In today’s increasingly competitive real estate market, Home Staging has become an essential component of property marketing. Yet despite the growing recognition of the profession, many people still misunderstand what a professional Home Stager actually does.

Some view Home Staging as decorating. Others believe it is simply arranging furniture or adding accessories before a property goes on the market. While presentation is certainly part of the process, professional Home Staging is far more strategic. A Professional Home Stager is a marketing specialist who uses design principles, buyer psychology, and market knowledge to help properties appeal to the broadest possible audience.

Beyond Decorating

Interior designers create spaces tailored to the tastes and lifestyles of those who will live in them. Home Stagers, by contrast, prepare properties for sale.
Their objective is not to personalize a space, but rather to depersonalize it strategically so that prospective buyers can envision themselves living there.
Every recommendation made by a Home Stager serves a purpose: highlighting strengths, minimizing distractions, improving flow, enhancing perceived value, and creating an emotional connection with potential buyers.

Education and Training Matter

Like any profession, Home Staging requires specialized knowledge and continuous learning. As markets evolve, professionals continue to refine their skills through advanced training, certification programs, conferences, and professional associations.

Professional Home Stagers invest in education to develop expertise in:
•⁠  ⁠Buyer psychology
•⁠  ⁠Real estate marketing
•⁠  ⁠Property presentation
•⁠  ⁠Color and design principles
•⁠  ⁠Space planning
•⁠  ⁠Visual merchandising
•⁠  ⁠Business practices
•⁠  ⁠Industry ethics

Understanding the Real Estate Industry

Professional Home Stagers do not work in isolation. They collaborate closely with real estate agents, brokers, developers, investors, photographers, and property owners.
To provide meaningful value, a Home Stager must understand:

•⁠  ⁠Local market conditions
•⁠  ⁠Buyer expectations
•⁠  ⁠Pricing strategies
•⁠  ⁠Marketing trends
•⁠  ⁠Property positioning

This broader perspective allows Home Stagers to make recommendations that support the overall sales strategy rather than focusing solely on aesthetics.

Professional Ethics and Standards

A defining characteristic of any profession is a commitment to ethical practice.
Professional Home Stagers understand the importance of honesty, transparency, respect for clients, and adherence to industry standards.
Professional associations play a vital role in establishing these standards, providing education, encouraging accountability, and supporting the growth of the industry worldwide.

The Value of Certification

Certification demonstrates a commitment to professional development and excellence.
While requirements vary across organizations and regions, certification typically signifies that an individual has completed structured training and has demonstrated a level of competency in the profession. For clients and industry partners, certification provides confidence that the Home Stager follows recognized standards and best practices.

The Future of Professional Home Staging

As real estate marketing continues to evolve, the role of the Home Stager is becoming increasingly important.
Today’s buyers begin their property search online. First impressions are often formed through photographs, videos, virtual tours, and social media content long before a buyer steps through the front door.
Professional Home Stagers help ensure that those first impressions are positive, memorable, and effective.
The profession continues to grow around the world, driven by increasing consumer awareness and a greater understanding of the impact presentation has on property sales.

Raising the Standard Together

The future of Home Staging depends on education, professionalism, and collaboration. As the industry matures, Professional Home Stagers will continue to play an essential role in helping sellers, real estate professionals, and buyers achieve better outcomes.
At GAPHS, we believe that education, ethical standards, certification, and international collaboration are key to advancing the profession and strengthening its global reputation.

title: London Design Festival 2026: Why It Matters for the Global Design & Home Staging Community
excerpt: Every September, London becomes something more than a city. It becomes a living laboratory of creativity.
body:
Every September, London becomes something more than a city. It becomes a living laboratory of creativity.
From 12–20 September 2026, the London Design Festival (LDF) returns, transforming the British capital into a global stage for design, architecture, innovation, and cultural exchange.

Recognised as one of the world’s leading design events, LDF is not a single exhibition but an ecosystem of installations, talks, exhibitions, trade showcases, and city-wide activations spread across London’s most iconic districts and creative hubs.

For professionals in home staging, interior design, real estate, and spatial storytelling, this is not simply an event to visit, it is an event to experience, study, and translate into practice.

Why the London Design Festival Matters for Home Staging Professionals

The Home Staging profession sits at the intersection of design, psychology, and real estate value creation. LDF offers a rare opportunity to observe all three in their most advanced form.

⁠
A global pulse of design innovation

LDF brings together designers, architects, product developers, and cultural institutions from around the world, making it one of the most important reference points for emerging global trends.

For Home Stagers, this means direct exposure to:

•⁠  ⁠New material languages
•⁠  ⁠Future colour directions
•⁠  ⁠Evolving spatial concepts
•⁠  ⁠Experimental approaches to light, form, and emotion

⁠London as a “live showroom”

Unlike traditional fairs, LDF activates the entire city. Streets, museums, galleries, studios, and public spaces become part of the exhibition itself.

This urban format offers a powerful learning model:

•⁠  ⁠How design performs in real-life environments
•⁠  ⁠How people emotionally respond to spatial interventions
•⁠  ⁠How storytelling can transform ordinary spaces into memorable experiences

For Home Staging professionals, this is the closest equivalent to a real-world “macro staging laboratory.”

⁠Installations that redefine emotional space

One of the defining characteristics of the festival is its large-scale installations, often immersive, conceptual, and emotionally driven.

These works frequently explore:

•⁠  ⁠Sustainability and circular design
•⁠  ⁠Light as architectural material
•⁠  ⁠Cultural identity and narrative space
•⁠  ⁠Human interaction within designed environments

Such installations are especially relevant to staging, where emotional impact is often more powerful than structural change.

A convergence of design disciplines

LDF is not limited to interiors. It integrates:

•⁠  ⁠Architecture
•⁠  ⁠Product and furniture design
•⁠  ⁠Fashion and material innovation
•⁠  ⁠Digital and speculative design

This multidisciplinary approach reflects a critical reality: modern interiors are no longer isolated environments—they are curated ecosystems influenced by multiple creative industries.

A strategic opportunity for professional positioning

For GAPHS members and home staging professionals, attending LDF is not only inspirational, it is strategic.

It allows professionals to:

•⁠  ⁠Strengthen design authority and creative credibility
•⁠  ⁠Build international networks across creative industries
•⁠  ⁠Translate global trends into local market advantage
•⁠  ⁠Elevate the perceived value of staging within real estate ecosystems

In a market where differentiation is increasingly defined by visual intelligence and storytelling capability, exposure to events like LDF becomes a competitive asset.

Key Highlights of the Festival Experience

While the full programme evolves annually, the structure of the festival typically includes:

•⁠  ⁠City-wide installations across London districts
•⁠  ⁠Curated design routes and neighbourhood “design districts”
•⁠  ⁠Talks and panels with global thought leaders
•⁠  ⁠Experimental exhibitions and pop-up environments
•⁠  ⁠Trade-focused showcases and design launches
•⁠  ⁠Institutional collaborations with leading museums and galleries

Each layer of the festival contributes to a broader narrative: design is not an object—it is a system of experience.

Final Reflection

The London Design Festival continues to reinforce London’s position as one of the world’s most influential design capitals. More importantly, it demonstrates how design is evolving—from aesthetics to strategy, from decoration to meaning, and from objects to experiences.

For the global home staging community, this shift is essential.

Because staging today is no longer about furnishing a property. It is about constructing an emotional and commercial narrative that resonates instantly, across cultures and markets.

London Design Festival is therefore not only an event to attend, but a lens through which we can better understand the future of spatial experience.

title: The ROI conversation: how to stop selling staging as a cost
excerpt: Every home stager knows the moment. You have presented a beautiful concept, the seller loves it, and then comes the question: "But isn't that quite expensive?"
body:
Every home stager knows the moment. You have presented a beautiful concept, the seller loves it, and then comes the question: "But isn't that quite expensive?"

In that single statement, months of expertise get reduced to a line item. The mood in the room shifts. You find yourself defending a number instead of discussing an outcome, and whatever happens next, you are now negotiating from a weaker position than the one you occupied thirty seconds earlier.

The problem is rarely the price. The value has not yet been framed as a return. The most successful stagers are not necessarily the most creative ones. They are the ones who can translate their work into the language their clients actually care about: time on market, sale price, and risk.

This is a learnable skill. It has less to do with charisma than with preparation, and it begins long before anyone brings up a figure.
Staging is marketing, not decoration.
When a seller sees staging as "making the house pretty," it competes with every other discretionary expense in their life. A new kitchen. A holiday. A cushion against the uncertainty of moving. In that mental category, staging will always be the first thing to be cut because it feels optional.

When they see it as marketing, the single most valuable asset they own, the conversation changes entirely. Nobody sells a company without a prospectus. Nobody launches a product without packaging. Yet sellers routinely put a property worth hundreds of thousands on the market with no thought given to how it will be perceived in the two seconds a buyer spends scrolling past it online.

A staged home photographs better, shows better, and gives buyers a story to step into. You are not decorating a room. You are shortening the distance between the listing and the offer.
Reframing your service this way is the first and most important shift, and it costs you nothing. It also determines how the rest of the conversation goes. A decorator justifies a price. A marketing partner discusses a strategy.
Know the numbers, and make them the client's numbers.
You do not need to quote dubious statistics to make the case. Sellers have learned to discount averages, and rightly so. The property down the road is not their property.
What you need instead is to make the math personal. Ask two questions.

What does one month of carrying this property cost you? Add up mortgage interest, local taxes, energy, insurance, maintenance, and, where relevant, the cost of running two households at once. Sellers almost never have this number ready. Watching them calculate it out loud is often the most persuasive moment in the entire meeting because you did not tell them anything. They told themselves.

And what does a single price reduction usually look like in this segment? Not a hypothetical one. The real thing. In most markets, the first reduction is not a token gesture. It is a meaningful percentage, made under pressure, after the listing has already lost its momentum.
When a seller realizes that avoiding a price drop or a few weeks on the market can exceed the entire staging investment, the objection dissolves. Staging stops being an expense and becomes insurance against a slow, discounted sale.
There is a second effect worth naming. A property that attracts more viewings creates competition, and competition changes who holds the leverage in a negotiation. That is difficult to quantify precisely, which is why it belongs in the conversation as a principle rather than a promise. Presentation determines how many people feel they are being spoken to. The number of people who feel spoken to determines the pressure in the room.
Timing matters more than most stagers think.
The ROI conversation cannot be retrofitted. If the first substantive thing a client hears from you is a quote, you have already agreed to be evaluated on price.
Lead with the strategy. Talk about the property's position in the market, who the likely buyer is, and what will make that buyer act quickly. Discuss the photographs before the furniture, because they are what most buyers will actually see. By the time you present a figure, the client should already understand what the figure is buying.
This is also why the strongest stagers involve themselves early, ideally before the property is listed and certainly before it has sat unsold for two months. A relaunch is always harder than a launch. A listing that has been on the market too long carries a history of its own, and it is not a flattering one.
Presentation quality protects the return.
The ROI argument only applies if the result delivers.
A half-furnished room with mismatched pieces weakens the very premium you are promising. A small sofa in a large living room does not read as restraint. It reads as a compromise, and buyers register that instantly, even when they cannot articulate why. This is where the quality and coherence of your collection directly affect your credibility.
To defend a professional fee, you need a professional presentation: current pieces, the right scale, materials that read as quality on camera and in person. Scale, in particular, is unforgiving. Generous rooms demand generous furniture, and the moment the proportions are wrong, the room communicates uncertainty rather than value.
The gap between "nicely furnished" and "clearly desirable" is exactly the gap the buyer pays for. It is also the gap that justifies your fee. Sell an ROI you cannot demonstrate, and the argument collapses on the second project when the client compares the promise to the result.
Selling ROI without inflating your own costs
Here is the tension that sits underneath all of this.
Delivering a return-worthy result usually means access to more and better inventory than any single project can justify owning. The luxury segment is especially punishing in this respect. The statement pieces that make a villa work are precisely the pieces that will sit unused between projects, and the storage, insurance, transport, and handling they require do not pause while they wait.
Buying it all inflates your fixed costs and quietly erodes the very margin the ROI story is supposed to protect. Worse, it distorts your judgment. A stager who owns a warehouse full of furniture is under constant pressure to use that furniture, whether or not it is right for the property in front of them. The inventory starts making the design decisions.
The smarter route is to keep your costs variable. Bring in exactly the collection each project needs, only when you need it. Scale up when a large project arrives and scale down when it ends. Your client gets the premium result. You keep your risk low, your pricing honest, and your creative choices genuinely free.
How The Staging Company fits in
The Staging Company works alongside home stagers as exactly this kind of partner.
We provide access to a broad, current collection and handle the logistics: transport, installation, and dismantling. That means you can promise a high-end, return-driven result without carrying the inventory or the operational load. No warehouse. No lease. No van. No weekend spent assembling flat-pack furniture in an empty villa.
You keep the client relationship and the creative direction. We give it a foundation that holds up to scrutiny.
It also changes what you can say yes to. Two projects in the same week, a property twice the size of anything you have staged before, a deadline that would be impossible with your own logistics: these stop being reasons to decline and start being reasons to be chosen.
The return is the point.
Staging has never really been about furniture.
It is about helping a property sell faster, for more, with less risk, and helping your client see that before they sign. Every element of the work, from the moodboard to the last cushion, exists to serve that outcome. The furniture is simply the instrument.
Master the ROI conversation, and you stop competing on price. You stop being the line item that gets cut when the budget tightens. You start being hired for the outcome you create by clients who understand what they are buying and why it is worth it.
That shift is available to every stager reading this. It requires no new qualification and no larger warehouse. It requires only that you learn to speak about your work in the terms your clients already use when they think about their property: what it will sell for, how long it will take, and what it will cost them if it does not.

Ready to make ROI your strongest sales argument?
The Staging Company provides the collection and logistical backbone to deliver results your clients can measure. Visit www.thestagingcompany.eu and get in touch.

title: The Psychology Behind Buyer Decisions
excerpt: When people purchase a home, they like to believe they are making a rational decision.
body:
When people purchase a home, they like to believe they are making a rational decision.
They compare prices, review market data, analyze locations, and calculate mortgage payments. Yet decades of research in consumer behavior suggest that buying decisions are rarely based on logic alone.

In reality, people buy emotionally and justify their decisions rationally afterward. Understanding this principle is one of the reasons Home Staging has become such a powerful tool in modern real estate marketing.

First Impressions Happen Fast

Research consistently shows that people form impressions within seconds of encountering a new environment.
Whether viewing online photographs, virtual tours, or attending a property showing in person, buyers begin making judgments almost immediately. These initial impressions influence how they perceive everything that follows.

A well-presented property creates a positive emotional response from the outset, making buyers more receptive to its features and benefits.
Conversely, clutter, poor maintenance, strong personal tastes, or distracting décor can create negative impressions that are difficult to overcome, regardless of the property’s actual value.

The Power of Emotional Connection

Homes are unlike most purchases.
A buyer is not simply purchasing walls, floors, and square footage. They are purchasing the possibility of a future life. They imagine family gatherings in the dining room, relaxing evenings in the living room, celebrations in the kitchen, and personal milestones within the space. The stronger this emotional connection becomes, the more likely a buyer is to develop a genuine interest in the property.
Professional Home Staging helps create an environment where these emotional connections can occur naturally. By presenting a property in its best light, Home Stagers help buyers focus on possibilities rather than distractions.

Cognitive Overload and Decision Fatigue

Today’s consumers are overwhelmed by choices.
In many markets, buyers may view dozens of listings online before deciding which properties to visit in person. When people are faced with excessive information or visual clutter, decision-making becomes more difficult. Psychologists refer to this as cognitive overload. A cluttered or poorly organized property forces buyers to process unnecessary information, reducing their ability to appreciate the home’s strengths.

Professional Home Staging simplifies the visual experience.
Clean, organized, and thoughtfully arranged spaces allow buyers to absorb information more easily and focus on what matters most.

The Role of Visual Perception

Human beings are highly visual creatures.Our brains process visual information significantly faster than written information, making appearance a critical factor in decision-making.
Well-balanced furniture placement, strategic lighting, harmonious color palettes, and carefully curated accessories can influence how large, bright, welcoming, or functional a space feels.
Importantly, perception often carries as much weight as reality. A room does not necessarily need to be larger to feel larger. A property does not need additional windows to feel brighter.
Through strategic presentation, Home Staging enhances how buyers perceive the space.

The Principle of Social Proof

People naturally look for cues that help them determine value. A beautifully presented home communicates that the property has been cared for and maintained.
Buyers often interpret this visual signal as evidence that the home is desirable. This phenomenon, known as social proof, influences purchasing decisions across industries and plays an important role in real estate. A staged property often appears more desirable because it visually demonstrates its potential and reinforces its perceived value.

Online Psychology Matters More Than Ever

For many buyers, the first showing takes place online. Property photographs, videos, social media posts, and virtual tours frequently determine whether a buyer decides to schedule an in-person visit. In this environment, presentation has become even more important.
Home Staging is no longer limited to preparing properties for physical showings. It is equally about creating compelling visual marketing assets that capture attention in crowded digital marketplaces. A strong first impression online can significantly increase engagement and buyer interest.

The Science Behind the Strategy

Home Staging is often associated with design and aesthetics, but its effectiveness is rooted in psychology. The goal is not decoration for decoration’s sake.
The goal is to create an environment that supports positive first impressions, reduces distractions, encourages emotional engagement, and allows buyers to envision a future within the home. When buyers feel connected to a property, they are more likely to remember it, revisit it, and ultimately make an offer.

Understanding Human Behavior

At its core, Home Staging is about understanding people. It recognizes that buyers are not purely logical decision-makers and that perception, emotion, and experience all influence purchasing behavior. By combining design principles with an understanding of buyer psychology, Professional Home Stagers help bridge the gap between a property’s potential and a buyer’s imagination.
That is why Home Staging continues to be one of the most effective tools available in real estate marketing today.
Because homes are not sold solely through facts and figures. They are sold through the feelings they inspire.

“Home Staging is often perceived as a design service, but at its core it is a marketing discipline rooted in human behavior. When we understand how buyers think, feel, and make decisions, we can create spaces that communicate value more effectively.” — Sanja Radovanovic, President, GAPHS

title: Home Staging vs Interior Design: Understanding the Difference
excerpt: Home Staging and Interior Design are often confused with one another.
body:
Home Staging and Interior Design are often confused with one another.

Both involve creating attractive spaces. Both require an understanding of color, furniture, layout, and visual appeal. Yet despite these similarities, they are distinct professions with different objectives, clients, and measures of success.
Understanding the difference helps property owners, real estate professionals, and consumers choose the right service for their needs.

Different Goals

The most important distinction between Home Staging and Interior Design lies in their purpose.
Interior Design focuses on creating a space that reflects the needs, preferences, and lifestyle of the people who will live in it.
Home Staging, on the other hand, prepares a property for sale or rent. The objective is not to personalize the home, but to make it appealing to the broadest possible audience of potential buyers or tenants.

While an Interior Designer asks, “How can this space work best for the homeowner?”

A Home Stager asks, “How can this space appeal to the marketplace?”

Different Clients

Interior Designers typically work with homeowners, businesses, hospitality operators, or organizations seeking to create functional and aesthetically pleasing environments for long-term use.

Home Stagers often work with:

•⁠  ⁠Property sellers
•⁠  ⁠Real estate agents
•⁠  ⁠Property developers
•⁠  ⁠Investors
•⁠  ⁠Builders
•⁠  ⁠Landlords

Their focus is on maximizing a property’s marketability and perceived value during the selling or leasing process.

Personalization vs Neutralization

Interior Design celebrates personal expression. Designers often incorporate a client’s favorite colors, collections, furniture styles, hobbies, and lifestyle preferences into the final design.

Home Staging takes a different approach.
Because buyers need to envision themselves living in the property, Home Stagers typically recommend reducing highly personal elements and creating a more universally appealing presentation. This process is not about removing character. It is about removing barriers that might prevent potential buyers from forming an emotional connection with the home.

Living in the Home vs Selling the Home

An Interior Designer creates a space for daily living. Comfort, personal functionality, family routines, and individual preferences are central considerations.
A Home Stager creates a space designed to support a marketing objective. Every decision is made with one question in mind:
“Will this help the property perform better in the marketplace?” Furniture placement, room function, accessory selection, lighting, and styling choices are all evaluated through the lens of buyer perception.

Different Measures of Success

The success of an Interior Design project is typically measured by client satisfaction, functionality, aesthetics, and long-term enjoyment of the space.
The success of a Home Staging project is measured differently.

Indicators may include:

•⁠  ⁠Increased buyer interest
•⁠  ⁠More property showings
•⁠  ⁠Stronger online engagement
•⁠  ⁠Reduced time on market
•⁠  ⁠Improved perceived value
•⁠  ⁠Competitive offers

While beautiful presentation is important, it is ultimately a means to achieve a business and marketing objective.

The Role of Psychology

Both professions rely on an understanding of human behavior, but Home Staging places particular emphasis on buyer psychology.
Professional Home Stagers study how consumers perceive space, process visual information, and make purchasing decisions.
Their recommendations are designed to help buyers focus on a property’s strengths while minimizing distractions that could negatively influence first impressions.
This marketing-oriented approach is one of the defining characteristics of Home Staging as a profession.

Complementary, Not Competing Professions

It is important to recognize that Home Staging and Interior Design are not competing disciplines. In fact, many professionals collaborate successfully across both fields.
A property may benefit from Home Staging before it is sold and later benefit from Interior Design once the new owners move in.
Each profession serves a different purpose at a different stage of a property’s journey. Both contribute value, but in distinct ways.

Choosing the Right Service

If your goal is to create a home that reflects your personality, lifestyle, and long-term needs, an Interior Designer may be the right choice.
If your goal is to prepare a property for sale or rent and position it effectively in the marketplace, a Professional Home Stager can help maximize its appeal to prospective buyers or tenants.
Understanding this distinction allows consumers and real estate professionals to make informed decisions and achieve better results.

More Than Beautiful Spaces

At first glance, Home Staging and Interior Design may appear similar. Both create attractive environments. Both require creativity, expertise, and attention to detail.
However, their objectives are fundamentally different.

Interior Design is about the people who live in a space. Home Staging is about the people who may choose to buy it.
One creates a home for living. The other creates a home that inspires someone to say, “This is the one.”

Jennie Norris, CEO and Chairwoman of the International Association of Home Staging Professionals, will also participate as an international speaker.
The conference will provide an opportunity to encounter different professional perspectives, explore practices emerging across individual markets and strengthen dialogue among professionals working within diverse cultural and real estate contexts.

For GAPHS, this international exchange is fundamental to the evolution of the profession. From knowledge to practice: the Eurasian Home Staging Championship

Home Stagers, real estate agents, property owners, investors and property-flipping professionals will work in multidisciplinary teams to develop a complete Home Staging proposal for a real apartment.

Within three hours, each team will be required to analyse the property, define its commercial objective and develop a coherent concept designed to prepare it for a more profitable sale or rental. Participants will create visual proposals, consider budgets and product selection, and present the strategy behind their decisions.

The projects will then be presented to a judging panel composed of investors and evaluated according to two central criteria:

* rationality and commercial viability;
* strength and originality of the concept.

The Championship highlights an essential principle of professional Home Staging: creativity must be connected to strategy. An effective project is not solely an aesthetic exercise; it must respond to the property, its target audience, its intended position within the market and the commercial result it is expected to support.

By bringing together professionals with different backgrounds and levels of experience, the initiative also creates a valuable environment for collaborative learning, knowledge exchange and new professional connections.

Recognising excellence through the Eurasian Home Stagers Awards

First, second and third place will be recognised in each category, alongside additional special distinctions presented by jury members and event partners.

Building a more connected international profession

GAPHS’s support of the Eurasian Home Stagers Summit reflects the Association’s commitment to creating meaningful connections between Home Staging communities, encouraging professional exchange and increasing the international visibility of the profession.

“The growth of Home Staging as a recognised profession depends upon our ability to learn from one another, build bridges between markets and create opportunities for professionals to exchange both knowledge and experience.
The Eurasian Home Stagers Summit brings these elements together through education, practical collaboration and professional recognition. GAPHS is proud to support an initiative that strengthens international dialogue and contributes to the continued evolution of our industry.”

 — Sanja Radovanovic, President of GAPHS

Events of this nature demonstrate the value of bringing different markets into the same conversation. They allow professionals to recognise shared challenges, discover new approaches and contribute collectively to a stronger, more visible and increasingly connected global industry.

GAPHS looks forward to joining the international Home Staging community in October and supporting an event designed to advance knowledge, celebrate professional excellence and create new opportunities for collaboration.
